title: India
hookLine: three Jewish communities in India: the Bene Israel, the Jews of Cochin, and Baghdadi Jews

cards: In villages along India's western coast, neighbors once had a name for a group of families who pressed oil for a living. They called them the Saturday oil-pressers, because on Saturdays their presses stood still.

Nobody worked, nobody lit a fire. The families did not have Torah scrolls or rabbis. What they had, tradition says, was the habit of resting on the seventh day, and one line they never stopped saying.

teach.h: THE BENE ISRAEL KEEP THE SHEMA.
teach.b: The first community is the Bene Israel, the children of Israel. Their own tradition says their ancestors were shipwrecked on the Konkan coast long ago, and lost their books in the sea.
They kept what they could: Shabbat, circumcision, some of the festivals, and the Shema. "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." Tradition says they said it at every turn of life.
Later, teachers from elsewhere helped them reconnect with the wider Jewish world, and families moved to Bombay.
The second community lived on the southwest coast, in Cochin, in Kerala. Cochin Jews were traders along the spice routes.
Tradition says a local ruler once gave a Jewish leader named Joseph Rabban copper plates granting rights to his community.
In the old quarter of Kochi stands the Paradesi Synagogue, its floor laid with hand-painted blue and white tiles from China, brass lamps hanging above.
Cochin Jewish women sang their own songs in Malayalam, the language of Kerala.

The third community is the Baghdadi Jews. Yes, Baghdad, from a few days ago. Traders from Iraq and nearby lands settled in Bombay and Calcutta, spoke Arabic and later English, and built synagogues and schools.
Three communities, three histories, one country. Since then, families from all three have moved to Israel and elsewhere, and small communities remain.
And each of the three, in its own language and its own way, made a home among its neighbors.

how: Bene Israel families keep their own customs, such as the malida offering of flattened rice in honor of Elijah; the Paradesi Synagogue in Kochi still stands, and Jews of Indian descent in Israel and elsewhere keep their communities' songs and foods.

games.q: you are a Bene Israel oil-presser. it is Saturday morning, and your neighbors expect oil. what do you do?
games.why: their presses stood still on Saturdays, so their neighbors called them the Saturday oil-pressers.

practice: Picture the Paradesi Synagogue: blue and white tiles, each painted by hand, brass lamps overhead.
Let your eyes rest on one tile, like the others and not quite the same, and think of the people in your life who are like that: part of a pattern, and each their own.
